title: Preparing people for procedures and hospital
blurb: Plan a hospital visit or procedure with social stories, visual schedules, pre-visits and graded exposure, and share difficult news accessibly.
question: Aiden, 34, is autistic and has a learning disability. He needs a blood test and has run out of the clinic twice before. What adjustments should the learning disability nurse plan before the next appointment?

teach.body: Unfamiliar places, people, noise, waiting and touch can make hospital frightening for people with a learning disability and autistic people. Preparing them is part of the Equality Act duty to make reasonable adjustments, and part of taking 'all practicable steps' to help someone make their own decision under the Mental Capacity Act. In plain English: if a person knows what will happen, where, with whom and in what order, they are far more likely to cope and to consent.
teach.cite: Equality Act 2010 s20; Mental Capacity Act 2005 s1(3)

head: Tool
What it does
rows: Describes the event step by step
Shows the order of the day in pictures
Meets the place and staff in advance
Tells staff what matters to the person
teach.caption: Most plans combine several tools, agreed with the person and those who know them.

teach.body: Social Stories were created by Carol Gray in 1991 to describe a situation, event or activity for autistic people, so they know what to expect. They are used to prepare for procedures and hospital visits. For autistic adults, NICE CG142 1.1.8 recommends adjusting personal space, visual supports, wall colours, lighting and noise. For autistic children and young people (under 19), NICE CG170 recommends similar environmental adjustments (1.1.9) and appointments at the beginning or end of the day to minimise waiting (1.1.10). For an adult, a first or last appointment is a reasonable adjustment under the Equality Act rather than a NICE recommendation.
teach.cite: NICE CG142 1.1.8; NICE CG170 1.1.9-1.1.10; Equality Act 2010 s20

items.label: Ask the person, carers; read passport
First slot, quiet room, familiar person

teach.body: For a person with a fear of needles, masks or scanners, graded exposure (desensitisation) breaks the procedure into small steps: looking at a picture of the equipment, holding it, sitting in the chair, a tourniquet on, and so on, with praise and rest at each step. NICE NG54 recommends considering graded exposure techniques for anxiety and phobias in people with learning disabilities. It takes time, so start well before a non-urgent procedure.

teach.caption: Move on only when the person is comfortable at each step.

teach.h: Records that travel with the person

rows.label: Held by
values: The person, on paper or app

teach.caption: Learning disability liaison nurses help hospital teams read these records and plan adjustments before admission.

teach.body: People with a learning disability have a right to know about their own health, including serious illness and death. Plan with people who know the person; use their communication method, easy read and pictures; give small amounts at a time; use clear words such as 'died', not euphemisms like 'gone to sleep'; check understanding and come back to it. Grief and fear may show as changes in behaviour, so plan support afterwards.
teach.cite: NMC Annexe A 2.9; accessible information principles

teach.body: Aiden, 34, ran out of clinic twice. The learning disability nurse meets him and his support worker. They agree a social story with photos of the clinic and nurse, the first appointment of the day, a quiet side room and no waiting area. Over three weeks they use graded exposure: photos, a visit, then the tourniquet. On the day his familiar nurse takes blood with his chosen music. The plan and adjustments are recorded and flagged for next time.

teach.text: Do not leave preparation until the day, and do not treat running away as a settled, informed refusal: it may be fear of the unknown. Also avoid 'just this once' restraint or sedation for a non-urgent test when preparation has not been tried; that is not the least restrictive option.

items: Preparation is a reasonable adjustment and an MCA 'practicable step'.
Social stories (Carol Gray, 1991) and visual schedules show what will happen.
Visual supports and a calm environment (CG142 1.1.8 adults; CG170 1.1.9 under 19s); first or last appointments cut waiting (CG170 1.1.10).
Graded exposure for fears and phobias (NICE NG54 1.8.7).
Break difficult news in small steps, plain words, the person's own mode.

summary: You can now plan a hospital visit or procedure using social stories, visual schedules, pre-visits, graded exposure and timing adjustments, and use passports and the digital flag to share them. You can also break difficult news accessibly and plan support afterwards.

A.q: Lily, 22, is autistic and has a learning disability. She is anxious about an outpatient scan next month. Which tool is designed to describe what will happen, step by step, from her point of view?
options: A Social Story
A DisDAT form
An ABC chart
A health action plan
A.why: Social Stories, created by Carol Gray in 1991, describe a situation or event for autistic people so they know what to expect.

whyNot.1: DisDAT records signs of contentment and distress, not what will happen.
whyNot.2: ABC charts record behaviour and its context.
whyNot.3: A health action plan lists health actions from the annual health check.

A.q: NICE CG170 recommends which appointment adjustment for autistic young people to reduce distress?
options: Appointments in the middle of the clinic session
Appointments at the start or end of the day
Appointments with a different clinician each visit
Appointments made by letter with no reminder
A.why: CG170 recommends appointments at the start or end of the day to minimise waiting, alongside visual supports and attention to the environment.

whyNot.0: Mid-session slots are when waiting and busy rooms are most likely.
whyNot.3: Reminders help; removing them adds uncertainty.

A.q: Which NICE guideline recommends considering graded exposure techniques for anxiety or phobias in people with learning disabilities?
options: NICE NG11
NICE NG43
NICE NG54
NICE NG96
A.why: NICE NG54 1.8.7 recommends considering graded exposure techniques to treat anxiety symptoms or phobias in people with learning disabilities.

whyNot.1: NG43 covers transition from children's to adults' services.
whyNot.3: NG96 covers people growing older with learning disabilities.

B.q: Ravi, 40, has a learning disability and a fear of needles. He needs a non-urgent blood test. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Hold his arm still and take the blood quickly
Give oral sedation before the next appointment
Ask his brother to sign consent on his behalf
Use graded steps to build up to the blood test
B.why: For a non-urgent test, graded exposure with preparation is the least restrictive way to help him tolerate it (NICE NG54 1.8.7).

whyNot.0: Restraint for a non-urgent test without trying preparation is not least restrictive.
whyNot.1: Sedation is more restrictive and is not a first step for a non-urgent test.
whyNot.2: Ravi may well have capacity to decide for himself, and a relative cannot consent for an adult unless they hold a health and welfare lasting power of attorney and he lacks capacity.

B.q: A ward is admitting Erin, 27, who is autistic with a learning disability, for planned surgery. Which adjustment most directly reduces the uncertainty she finds distressing?
options: A visual schedule of her day agreed in advance
A bed in a busy bay near the nurses' station
A different nurse each shift for wider support
A standard admission leaflet given on arrival
B.why: A visual schedule shows what will happen and in what order, which reduces uncertainty; NICE CG142 1.1.8 recommends visual supports for autistic adults.

whyNot.1: A busy bay adds noise and unpredictability.
whyNot.3: A standard leaflet on arrival is too late and may not be accessible.

B.q: Which record is designed to make a disabled person's needed adjustments visible to NHS services across England through the national care record?
options: The hospital passport
The Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag
The health action plan
The Summary Care Record allergy field
B.why: The Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag records a person's reasonable adjustments on the national record; providers had to fully implement it by 30 September 2026.

whyNot.0: The passport is a valuable person-held document, not a national digital record.
whyNot.2: The health action plan lists health actions from the annual check.
whyNot.3: The allergy field records allergies, not reasonable adjustments.

C.q: Aiden, 34, is autistic with a learning disability. He ran out of the blood clinic twice. He agrees to try again. Which combination of adjustments is most appropriate?
options: Same clinic slot, a firmer explanation and a staff escort
Short-notice slot to reduce his time spent worrying
First slot, quiet room, social story and gradual steps
Home visit by an unfamiliar nurse without warning
C.why: Timing to avoid waiting, a quiet environment, a social story and graded exposure address the likely causes of his distress.

whyNot.0: Repeating the same conditions with an escort does not address the cause.
whyNot.1: Short notice removes preparation and increases uncertainty.
whyNot.3: An unannounced visit by a stranger adds unpredictability.

C.q: Bea, 51, has a moderate learning disability. Her mother has just died in hospital. Bea's sister asks the nurse how to tell her. Which advice is best?
options: Say her mother has gone to sleep and will not wake up
Wait until after the funeral so that Bea is not upset
Tell her that her mother has gone away for a long time
Use clear words such as 'died', with pictures and time
C.why: Clear words, in the person's communication mode, with time and repetition, help understanding. Euphemisms confuse and delaying the news excludes her from grieving.

whyNot.0: 'Gone to sleep' is a euphemism that can confuse and frighten.
whyNot.1: Delaying excludes Bea from the funeral and from grieving with her family.
whyNot.2: 'Gone away' suggests her mother may come back.

C.q: Nadia, 30, has a learning disability and needs a planned dental extraction under general anaesthetic. Her passport says she is frightened of masks. What is the most appropriate preparation?
options: Practise with a mask at home in small steps before the day
Apply the mask quickly on the day before she becomes upset
Leave the mask out of her social story to avoid alarming her
Plan to hold her still on the day while the mask is applied
C.why: Graded exposure to the mask well before the day, with praise, prepares her and is the least restrictive approach. Her social story should include the mask honestly.

whyNot.1: Surprising her with the mask increases fear and trust is lost.
whyNot.2: Leaving it out means the real event will not match what she expects.
whyNot.3: Holding her is restrictive and should not be the plan when preparation is possible.

reteach.title: No surprises
reteach.question: Imagine arriving somewhere strange where people touch you without warning. What would help you cope?

blocks.h: Know what, where, who and when
blocks.body: Most distress in hospital comes from the unknown. Tell the person what will happen, where, who will be there and in what order, using their own communication. Practise frightening parts in small steps beforehand. Choose times and places that avoid waiting and noise.

blocks.text: An honest social story includes the uncomfortable parts (the mask, the needle). Leaving them out breaks trust when they happen.

explain.body: Preparation is a reasonable adjustment and one of the practicable steps to support a person's own decision under the MCA.

test.q: Which principle of the Mental Capacity Act is most supported by preparing a person for a procedure?
options: Decisions in the person's best interests
The less restrictive option is considered
All practicable steps to help them decide
An unwise decision is not incapacity
test.why: MCA s1(3): a person is not treated as unable to decide unless all practicable steps to help them have been taken without success.

whyNot.0: Best interests applies only once a person lacks capacity.
whyNot.1: Less restrictive options matter, but preparation most directly supports the person's own decision.
whyNot.3: This principle concerns unwise choices, not preparation.

explain.body: Social stories describe an event; visual schedules show the order of the day. Both reduce uncertainty.

options: Dave Hewett
Andy Bondy
Lori Frost
Carol Gray
test.why: Carol Gray created Social Stories in 1991.

explain.body: Small steps towards a feared procedure, with praise and rest. NICE NG54 1.8.7: consider for anxiety and phobias.

test.q: During graded exposure for a needle phobia, when should the person move to the next step?
options: When they are comfortable at the current step
After a fixed number of practice sessions
When the appointment date gets close
When staff judge the step was long enough
test.why: Each step is repeated until the person is comfortable, then the next is introduced.

whyNot.1: A fixed count ignores how the person is coping.
whyNot.2: Rushing to meet a date undermines the method.
whyNot.3: Progress follows the person's comfort, not staff timing.

explain.body: Plan with people who know the person, use their communication method, plain words like 'died', small amounts, check and return to it.

test.q: Which phrase is best when telling a man with a learning disability that his father has died?
options: Dad has passed away
Dad has died
Dad has gone to sleep
Dad has gone to heaven
test.why: Plain words such as 'died' are clearer than euphemisms, which can confuse.

whyNot.0: 'Passed away' is a euphemism that may not be understood.
whyNot.2: 'Gone to sleep' can confuse and cause fear of sleep.
whyNot.3: Religious language may be meaningful, but first use plain words.
